In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of lead on the neuropsychological functioning of preschool children in the community.
the effects of chronic low-level exposure to lead on the neuropsychological development of children.

the relationship between lead exposure and neuropsychological functioning in young children living in an environment where lead levels are elevated but not sufficiently high to be associated with clinical lead poisoning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuropsychological dysfunction in the lead-exposed children was mild and was confined to the performance scale of the W.I.S.C., and to the tapping test.

low-level lead absorption in children is not associated with significant changes in behaviour, and that it is associated with only a mild and selective impairment of cognitive function, which is most marked in the area of motor performance.
the children with low-level lead absorption had significantly lower performance I.Q. and significantly slowed motor function, but not significantly increased hyperactivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

lead absorption of 40-60 mug. per 1oo ml. has a specific effect on neuropsychological function that is independent of the effects of socioeconomic factors and of the general level of lead absorption in the population.
lead is a neurotoxin, but that the neurotoxicity is limited to specific functions, and not to the general level of intellectual ability.

the neuropsychological effects of low-level lead absorption in children may be subtle, but they are detectable by objective tests and may have a bearing on the interpretation of the results of other studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to do more research on the effects of lead on the developing brain and that we need to develop better ways to prevent lead exposure in children.
lead exposure is not a benign condition, and that it can cause significant harm to children.
